title: Newton's Law of Gravitation
notes: **Law statement:** every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force that is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres: $F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$.

**The universal constant G:** $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2/\text{kg}^2$. It is the same everywhere in the universe (hence 'universal') and was first measured by Cavendish (1798) using a torsion balance. G is very small, which is why the gravitational attraction between everyday objects is imperceptible.

**Vector form & direction:** the force on mass m₁ due to m₂ is $F_{12} = -G\frac{m_1m_2}{r^2} \hat{r}_{12}$, directed along the line joining the centres, always attractive. Newton's third law applies: $F_{12} = -F_{21}$.

**Superposition:** when several masses act on one particle, the net force is the vector sum of the individual forces: $F_{\text{net}} = \sum F_i$. Each pair obeys the inverse-square law independently.

**Worked example — Earth and Moon:** $m_{\text{Earth}} = 6\times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$, $m_{\text{Moon}} = 7.4\times 10^{22} \text{ kg}$, $r = 3.84\times 10^8 \text{ m}$. $F = \frac{6.67\times 10^{-11} \times 6\times 10^{24} \times 7.4\times 10^{22}}{(3.84\times 10^8)^2} = 2.0\times 10^{20} \text{ N}$ — enough to hold the Moon in orbit.

**Gravitational field strength:** $g = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{GM}{r^2}$, the force per unit mass at a distance r from mass M. On Earth's surface $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$, which gives Earth's mass: $M = \frac{gR^2}{G} \approx 5.97\times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$.

**Why G is used in orbits:** equating gravitational force to centripetal force ($\frac{GMm}{r^2} = \frac{mv^2}{r}$) gives orbital velocity $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$ and period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}}$ — Kepler's third law follows directly.

**Important comparisons:** gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces — between two protons the gravitational force is $\sim 10^{-36}$ times the electric force — yet it dominates cosmology because mass adds up while electric charges cancel.
confusion: ❌ 'There is a force of gravity only near Earth.' ✅ Gravity acts between ANY two masses anywhere in the universe — it never switches off, it only weakens with the square of distance.
❌ 'G can change with temperature or medium.' ✅ G is a universal constant — independent of temperature, pressure, medium, or the objects involved.
❌ 'The force depends on the square of the distance — it dies quickly.' ✅ It dies as 1/r² but never reaches zero; at double distance the force is a quarter, at ten times it is one-hundredth.

❌ 'Heavier objects fall faster because gravity pulls them harder.' ✅ Gravity pulls harder on heavier objects ($F = mg$), but their acceleration is the same: $a = F/m = g$, hence all bodies in free fall accelerate equally (ignoring air resistance).

❌ 'Earth pulls the Moon but the Moon does not pull Earth.' ✅ The forces are equal and opposite (Newton's third law). Earth and Moon pull on each other with equal forces — the Moon's acceleration is larger because its mass is smaller.
❌ 'Inside Earth gravity stops.' ✅ Inside a uniform sphere, g decreases linearly with distance from the centre, reaching zero at the centre — it is not zero except exactly at the centre.

universalFacts: Isaac Newton published the law of gravitation in his Principia (1687), synthesising the work of Kepler and Galileo — it was the first unified theory of terrestrial and celestial mechanics.
The modern value of $G = 6.674\times 10^{-11}$ is still the least precisely known fundamental constant because gravity is so weak.
The inverse-square character of gravity was seen by Newton as proof that planets are pulled toward the Sun rather than pushed.
Gravity's weakness explains why everyday objects attract negligibly but planets, stars, and galaxies dominate large-scale structure.
The same law that keeps you on the ground also governs satellite orbits, tidal effects, and the orbits of binary stars.
examples: Two 1 kg masses 1 m apart: $F = 6.67\times 10^{-11} \text{ N}$ — a trillion times weaker than a single paperweight's weight.
Earth–Moon force $\approx 2\times 10^{20} \text{ N}$, enough to lift a mass of $\approx 2\times 10^{19} \text{ kg}$.
g at 6400 km altitude ($h = R$): $g' = g\left(\frac{R}{R+h}\right)^2 = 9.8/4 = 2.45 \text{ m/s}^2$.
Satellite at $r = 7\times 10^6 \text{ m}$: $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}} \approx 7.56 \text{ km/s}$ (low Earth orbit speed).

keyPoints: $F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$ — force is always attractive, proportional to both masses, inverse-square in distance.
$G = 6.67\times 10^{-11} \text{ N·m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ is universal and independent of environment.
$g = \frac{GM}{r^2}$ is the force per unit mass; on Earth's surface it is 9.8 m/s².
The law explains orbital motion, tides, and planetary orbits.
Gravity between everyday objects is negligible because G is tiny.
summary: Newton's law of gravitation states that every mass attracts every other mass with $F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$. The universal constant $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11} \text{ N·m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ couples mass and distance to force. The law gives the gravitational field $g = \frac{GM}{r^2}$, explains orbital motion ($v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}}$), and underpins all celestial mechanics.
specialNotes: Use the centre-to-centre distance in r — for spheres this is the distance between centres.
G is the same everywhere; g is NOT — it varies with location and height.
Newton's third law applies to gravity: the forces on the two masses are equal and opposite.
For points above Earth's surface use $g = \frac{GM}{(R+h)^2}$; inside use $g = g(1 - d/R)$.
NEB numericals commonly give m₁, m₂, r and ask for F; or ask for g at a height.
importantStatements: Every particle attracts every other particle with a force directly proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
The gravitational constant $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11} \text{ N·m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ is a universal constant of nature.
Gravitational force is always attractive and acts along the line joining the centres.
The gravitational field strength $g = \frac{GM}{r^2}$ equals the force per unit mass.
Newton's law of gravitation explains planetary orbits, satellites, and tides.
importantNotes: Use centre-to-centre distance in Newton's law — for spheres, that is the distance between the centres.
The gravitational force between two bodies is independent of the medium between them.
The force on a body at height h above Earth uses r = R + h.
Newton's third law always applies: the forces are equal and opposite on the two bodies.
examShortTricks: Doubling the distance quarters the force; halving it quadruples the force (inverse-square).
For g at height: $g' = g\left(\frac{R}{R+h}\right)^2$; at $h = R$, $g' = g/4$.
Memorise $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11} \text{ N·m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ — it will not be provided in exams.
Orbital speed around Earth: $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}} \approx 7.9 \text{ km/s}$ near the surface.
examNotes: Numericals on $F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$ are a certainty — drill at least five.
